title: "5. Make groups easy to tell apart"
---

- If there are multiple groups, a legend should clearly delineate between the groups or data should be labeled directly
  - Legend should be close to the data itself when possible
  - Legend should be in logical (e.g., no high school, high school, college, graduate degree) and/or consistent order (e.g., in order on graph)
- The colors and/or symbols on the graph should clearly delineate between different lines/groups

### Bad graph example: cannot distinguish between symbols

![](images/yougov-transport.png){width=70% fig-alt="YouGov dot plot of attitudes toward types of transport in eleven countries: the countries are marked with nearly identical gray dots, so they cannot be told apart."}

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss.dta", clear
(gss.dta | GSS 1972 - 2016 Data | DMV Workshop)

. 
. // 5.a - Overlay multiple densities for different groups
. twoway kdensity wages if degree==0 || ///
>        kdensity wages if degree==1 || ///
>        kdensity wages if degree==2 || ///
>        kdensity wages if degree==3 || ///
>        kdensity wages if degree==4 ||, ///
>        legend(order(1 "< High School" 2 "HS Degree" 3 "Junior College" ///
>               4 "College Degree" 5 "Grad Degree")) ///
>        ytitle("Density") xtitle("Hourly Wages") xlab(0(10)70) ///
>        title("[5.a] Kernel-Density Plots of Hourly Wages Based on Educational 
> Attainment") ///
>        subtitle("Densities are group specific")

```

![](fig/dmv-05_a-kdensity_groups.png){width=80% fig-alt="[5.a] Kernel density plots of hourly wages for five levels of education, each with its own color and line pattern: the less than high school curve peaks highest and earliest (near 7 dollars), and each higher degree peaks lower and farther to the right, with the graduate degree curve flattest and peaking near 20 dollars."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
library(foreign)            # load Stata datasets
library(ggplot2)            # main graphics package
library(dplyr)              # data manipulation tools
library(cleanplots)         # Mize's graphics scheme

## Use cleanplots colors, markers, lines, and theme for all graphs ##
cleanplots_defaults()
theme_update(plot.title.position = "plot")   # titles start at left edge of graph

# General Social Survey Data
gss <- droplevels(read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/gss.dta"))

# 5.a - Overlay multiple densities for different groups
# Use both colors and line patterns so the five groups are easy to tell apart
degree_labels <- c("< High School", "HS Degree", "Junior College",
                   "College Degree", "Grad Degree")

ggplot(filter(gss, !is.na(degree)), aes(x = wages, color = degree, linetype = degree)) +
  geom_density(key_glyph = "path") +
  labs(x = "Hourly Wages", y = "Density", color = "", linetype = "",
       title = "[5.a] Kernel-Density Plots of Hourly Wages Based on Educational Attainment",
       subtitle = "Densities are group specific") +
  scale_color_cleanplots(labels = degree_labels) +
  scale_linetype_cleanplots(labels = degree_labels) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(0, 70, 10))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](5-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){fig-alt='[5.a] Kernel density plots of hourly wages for five levels of education, each with its own color and line pattern: the less than high school curve peaks highest and earliest, and each higher degree peaks lower and farther to the right, with the graduate degree curve flattest.' width=80%}
:::
:::


:::

## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si.dta", clear
(Health and Retirement Study 1992-2022 - Cleaned for MCAP SI)

. egen byte in1992 = max(year == 1992), by(hhidpn)

. 
. * Value labels for year so coefplot labels each wave with its year
. levelsof year, local(yrs)
1992 1994 1996 1998 2000 2002 2004 2006 2008 2010 2012 2014 2016 2018 2020 2022

. foreach y of local yrs {
  2.     label define yearlab `y' "`y'", add
  3. }

. label values year yearlab

. 
. // 5.b - Mean cognitive test score by year, separately for men and women
. *coefplot offsets the groups so their confidence intervals do not overlap
. qui regress cog ibn.year if in1992 & woman == 0, nocons

. est store cog_men

. qui regress cog ibn.year if in1992 & woman == 1, nocons

. est store cog_wom

. 
. coefplot (cog_men, label("Men")) (cog_wom, label("Women")), ///
>     vertical ylabel(12(1)18) ///
>     xtitle("Year") ytitle("Cognitive test score") ///
>     title("[5.b] Performance on a cognitive test over time, by gender") ///
>     subtitle("Means and 95% confidence intervals")

```

![](fig/dmv-05_b-dot_cog_gender.png){width=80% fig-alt="[5.b] Mean cognitive test scores with 95% confidence intervals for men (red) and women (light blue) in each HRS wave from 1996 to 2020: scores decline over time for both, from about 16 to 13.5 for men and from about 17 to 14.5 for women, with women higher in every wave."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# Health and Retirement Study Data
hrs <- read.dta("https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si.dta")

# Quick work to flag only those included in first HRS wave
ids_1992 <- hrs %>%
  filter(year == 1992) %>%
  pull(hhidpn) %>% unique()

hrs_filtered <- hrs %>%
  filter(hhidpn %in% ids_1992)

# 5.b - Mean cognitive test score by year, separately for men and women
# position_dodge( ) offsets the groups so their confidence intervals do not overlap
dodge <- position_dodge(width = .5)

ggplot(filter(hrs_filtered, !is.na(cog)),
       aes(x = factor(year), y = cog, color = woman, group = woman)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2.5, position = dodge) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = "errorbar", width = .2, position = dodge) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Cognitive test score", color = "",
       title = "[5.b] Performance on a cognitive test over time, by gender",
       subtitle = "Means and 95% confidence intervals") +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(12, 18, 1)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(12, 18))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](5-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-2-1.png){fig-alt='[5.b] Mean cognitive test scores with 95% confidence intervals for men and women in each HRS wave from 1996 to 2020: scores decline over time for both, with women higher in every wave.' width=80%}
:::
:::

## General advice: color

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
The color scheme (sequence of colors) on your graph should work for you---not against you

- **Nominal** (unordered) color schemes are best when you want distinct visual separation for each aspect of the plot
  - E.g., For a nominal variable such as race/ethnicity or religion
- **Ordinal** (sequential) color schemes work best for representing data that has a natural order
  - E.g., Age groups (e.g., generations) or Likert response options
- **Diverging** color schemes have a natural midpoint and diverge to both extremes
  - E.g., Political views
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
![](images/color-schemes-healy.png){fig-alt="Example color schemes: sequential grayscale, sequential blue to gray, sequential terrain, diverging, and unordered hues."}

::: {.callout-note icon="false" appearance="simple"}
\*Color chart from [Healy 2018](http://socviz.co/lookatdata.html)
:::
:::
::::

- Color alone can usually be used to distinguish between approximately 4--5 different lines/markers (see the [color limits section below](#nominal-scheme-color-limits))
  - Once you have 5+, you should also distinguish between lines/markers with different patterns (e.g., solid/dashed) and/or symbols (e.g., o, △, ☐)
- The main colors on a graphic should be distinguishable even when printed in black & white
  - Most journals allow color figures for the online version
    - However, most only print in black & white
  - But if your color scheme also works in black & white, no need to make two figures (more in the [Graphics Themes section](7-audience.qmd#graphics-schemes-in-stata))
- Avoid combining red and green
  - Red-green colorblindness is by far the most common type of colorblindness, [affecting up to 8%](https://nei.nih.gov/health/color_blindness/facts_about) of men (more discussion of colorblind friendly colors in the [Graphics Themes section](7-audience.qmd#graphics-schemes-in-stata))

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}
## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. // 5.c - Many groups: cleanplots changes marker shapes in addition to color
. local plots

. forvalues d = 0/7 {
  2.     qui regress cog ibn.year if in1992 & degree == `d', nocons
  3.     est store cog_deg`d'
  4.     local lab : label (degree) `d'
  5.     local plots `plots' (cog_deg`d', label("`lab'"))
  6. }

. 
. coefplot `plots', vertical ylabel(10(2)20) ///
>     xtitle("Year") ytitle("Cognitive test score") ///
>     title("[5.c] Performance on a cognitive test over time, by education") ///
>     subtitle("Means and 95% confidence intervals")

```

![](fig/dmv-05_c-dot_cog_educ.png){width=80% fig-alt="[5.c] Mean cognitive test scores with 95% confidence intervals for eight education groups in each wave from 1996 to 2020, each group with its own color and marker shape: scores decline over time in every group, and groups with more education score higher: the no degree group falls from about 13.5 to about 11, while the law/md/phd group stays highest, between about 17 and 19.5."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 5.c - Many groups: need to change marker shapes in addition to color
dodge <- position_dodge(width = .8)

ggplot(filter(hrs_filtered, !is.na(cog), !is.na(degree)),
       aes(x = factor(year), y = cog, color = degree, shape = degree, group = degree)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "point", size = 2, position = dodge) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = "errorbar",
               width = 0.2, position = dodge) +
  labs(x = "Year",
       y = "Cognitive test score",
       color = "", shape = "",
       title = "[5.c] Performance on a cognitive test over time, by education",
       subtitle = "Means and 95% confidence intervals") +
  scale_shape_cleanplots() +
  scale_y_continuous(breaks = seq(10, 20, 2)) + coord_cartesian(ylim = c(10, 20))
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](5-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){fig-alt='[5.c] Mean cognitive test scores with 95% confidence intervals for eight education groups in each wave from 1996 to 2020, each group with its own color and marker shape: scores decline over time in every group, and groups with more education score higher.' width=80%}
:::
:::


:::

### Nominal scheme color limits

- With a nominal scheme, it is hard to distinguish more than about 6 colors and *"...the task of matching colors to categories becomes too burdensome to be useful..." ([Wilke 2019](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/index.html) p.234)*

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

### Creating figures considerate of colorblindness

- About 5% of the population has some form of colorblindness (red/green being the most common which is why you should always avoid having red and green together on your figure... looking at you **stcolor**)
  - This excellent website [Coloring for Colorblindness](https://davidmathlogic.com/colorblind/#%23C80000-%2382C0DF-%23808080-%23000000-%2305CECE-%23881161) lets you check your color schemes to see how they will be viewed for those who are colorblind
    - Below is an example for how the first four default **cleanplots** colors look to individuals with various types of colorblindness

![](images/colorblind-palette.png){width=50% fig-alt="The first four cleanplots colors (red, light blue, gray, black) as seen with typical vision and with protanopia, deuteranopia, and tritanopia: the four colors stay distinct in every column."}
![](images/colorblind-palette-dtnm.png){width=12% fig-alt="The same four colors as seen with deuteranomaly."}

### Nominal and ordinal color palettes

- Most graphics themes' palettes are nominal
  - I.e., They do not imply ordering by the color choices
  - **okabe_ito** and **cleanplots** are nominal palettes
- It is sometimes useful to use an ordinal palette to have the visual reflect the ordering in the variable (e.g., for educational degrees)
  - The [**viridis**](https://bids.github.io/colormap/) and [**cividis**](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0199239) palettes are my preferred ordinal palettes
    - In Stata, implemented with the [**cleanplots#** themes](/software/cleanplots/index.qmd#ordinal-color-palettes)
  - Note you should not use an ordinal palette for a nominal variable (falsely implies ordering)

::: {.column width="20%"}
![](images/viridis-palette.png){width=60% fig-alt="The viridis ordinal palette, running from yellow through green and teal to dark purple."}
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
![](images/ordinal-palette-race.png){fig-alt="Bar chart of a nominal race-ethnicity variable drawn in an ordinal palette, crossed out with a red X."}
:::

Should use a nominal palette for a race-ethnicity variable
:::

::::

## Stata

```{.stata-run}
. // 5.f - Ordinal (viridis) colors for an ordered variable: cleanplots8v scheme
. use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/hrs_si.dta", clear
(Health and Retirement Study 1992-2022 - Cleaned for MCAP SI)

. 
. graph bar (mean) dzcount, over(degree) asyvars showyvars legend(off) ///
>     yvaroptions(label(angle(45))) ///
>     ytitle("Count of chronic diseases") ///
>     title("[5.f] Average chronic disease count by educational attainment") ///
>     subtitle("Colors are from cleanplots ordinal viridis scheme") ///
>     scheme(cleanplots8v)

```

![](fig/dmv-05_f-color_viridis.png){width=80% fig-alt="[5.f] Bar chart of the average count of chronic diseases for eight education groups in ordinal viridis colors, from light yellow for no degree to dark purple for law/md/phd: the average falls from about 2.25 with no degree to about 1.6 for the highest degrees."}

## R


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
# 5.f - Ordinal (viridis) palette for an ordered variable
ggplot(filter(hrs, !is.na(dzcount), !is.na(degree)),
       aes(x = degree, y = dzcount, fill = degree)) +
  stat_summary(fun = mean, geom = "bar", width = 0.65) +
  stat_summary(fun.data = mean_cl_normal, geom = "errorbar", width = 0.2) +
  labs(x = "Educational degree",
       y = "Count of chronic diseases",
       title = "[5.f] Average chronic disease count by educational attainment",
       subtitle = "Colors are from viridis palette") +
  theme(legend.position = "none") +
  scale_fill_viridis_d(direction = -1)
```

::: {.cell-output-display}
![](5-groups_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-6-1.png){fig-alt='[5.f] Bar chart of the average count of chronic diseases for eight education groups in ordinal viridis colors, from light yellow for no degree to dark purple for law/md/phd, with 95% confidence intervals: the average falls as education rises.' width=80%}
:::

\*Note ordering of colors. Logic = darker, more saturated colors = more of construct
